situation:
You and your teammate are the director of procurement and the director of resident services at CROSSKEY CAMPUS COMMUNITIES, a student housing operator that manages roughly 9,000 beds across six university markets. The chief executive officer (judge), who arrived fourteen months ago, has asked the two of you to review an offer from CROSSKEY's largest supplier and to recommend what the company should do about it.

CROSSKEY is in the second year of a turnaround. Two years of falling occupancy and deferred maintenance left the company refinanced on tight terms, and its lenders now review cash every quarter. Resident services has spent the fall absorbing complaints about late furniture deliveries in two markets, and the small team fielding those calls is worn thin. The board has told leadership that this year's cash target is not negotiable.

VANTAGE FURNISHINGS, which supplies beds and case goods to every CROSSKEY property, has offered a single payment of $600,000 if CROSSKEY renews its supply agreement five years early and exclusively. VANTAGE is open about how it earns the money back: unit prices rise modestly across the five years. CROSSKEY's management agreements with its university partners pass furniture costs through to rent, so those increases would eventually reach students.

Those same university agreements require CROSSKEY to disclose and credit back any rebate or allowance a supplier pays it, and CROSSKEY's own vendor policy says the same. VANTAGE's draft contract calls the money a marketing allowance rather than a rebate. Counsel's reading is that no statute answers the question and nothing here is a crime, but that if a university challenged the payment, a civil court would decide what the disclosure clause covers.

Declining is not free either. VANTAGE has said it cannot offer the same value as a price reduction and would take the proposal to a competing operator if CROSSKEY passes, ending a supply relationship built over eleven years. The chief executive officer (judge) wants the two of you to weigh taking the payment against negotiating lower unit prices instead, and to say what the universities should be told and how the money should be recorded.

You will present your recommendation and your reasoning to the chief executive officer (judge) in the CEO's office. The CEO (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and have answered any questions the CEO may have, the CEO (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer of CROSSKEY CAMPUS COMMUNITIES. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have asked the director of procurement and the director of resident services to weigh VANTAGE FURNISHINGS' $600,000 payment against negotiating lower unit prices instead, to recommend which course CROSSKEY takes, and to tell you what the university partners should be told and how the money should be recorded.

After the participants have presented their recommendation, you are to ask the following questions of each team:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, what would tell us we made the right call?
If someone outside the company asked about this payment later, what would we point to?
